title: What Amsterdam Knew About Money
dek: How a merchant city built trusted money, then spent it

slides.heading: Fix the Coin First
slides.body: By 1609 the Dutch Republic was full of clipped and foreign coin of uncertain weight. Amsterdam responded by founding the Wisselbank, a municipal exchange bank that credited deposits at their assayed value (van Dillen, *History of the Principal Public Banks*).

art.title: Isabella of Bourbon, Wife of Philip IV of Spain
art.artist: Workshop of Diego Rodriguez de Velázquez

slides.heading: Route Big Payments Through One Ledger
slides.body: Bills of exchange of 600 guilders or more had to be settled through Wisselbank accounts. Large merchants had to keep balances there, so the city's biggest payments cleared by book transfer instead of moving coin (Quinn and Roberds).

slides.heading: Reliable Money Commands a Premium
slides.body: Bank money traded above circulating coin. In his digression on banks of deposit in *The Wealth of Nations*, Adam Smith explains this premium, the agio: a bank florin had a known value and could not be stolen.

art.title: Still Life with Ostrich Egg Cup and the Whitfield Heirlooms

slides.heading: Receipts Turned Coin Into Credit
slides.body: From 1683 depositors of coin received tradable receipts, and accounts could no longer simply be cashed out. Quinn and Roberds argue this made bank money something close to modern central bank money. Not every historian accepts that framing.
slides.art_query: Rembrandt Syndics of the Drapers Guild

art.title: The Syndics of the Amsterdam Drapers' Guild, known as the ‘Sampling Officials’

slides.heading: Markets Need Rules Against Raids
slides.body: In 1609 a group around Isaac Le Maire sold VOC shares forward in a bear raid. In 1610 the States General banned selling shares the seller did not own. Lodewijk Petram, *The World's First Stock Exchange*, shows that traders kept finding ways around the ban.

art.title: Interior of the Oude Kerk, Delft

slides.heading: Cheap Debt Is Built on Trust
slides.body: Holland paid interest on its provincial bonds, the renten, reliably for generations. James Tracy traces this back to Habsburg-era reforms of the mid-1500s. De Vries and van der Woude, *The First Modern Economy*, show rates falling to around 4 percent by the mid-1600s.
slides.source: Tracy 1985; de Vries and van der Woude 1997

slides.heading: Secret Loans Break the Ledger
slides.body: In the 1780s the Wisselbank quietly lent large sums to the struggling VOC and to the city. As this became known, the agio collapsed and bank money traded at a discount. Quinn and Roberds describe this as the death of a reserve currency.

art.title: The Town Hall on Dam Square, Amsterdam

caption:
In 1609 Amsterdam built the most trusted money in Europe. Two centuries later it lent that trust to a failing company.
The Wisselbank turned unreliable coin into a sound bank money that traded at a premium (Smith 1776). In the 1780s, secret lending to the VOC broke the arrangement (Quinn and Roberds 2016). Petram (2014) shows that the city's stock market had to learn its own rules the hard way.

risk_notes: Wisselbank founding motive: currency disorder is the standard account (van Dillen). Say 'responded to' rather than claiming it was the only cause.
600 guilder threshold: this comes from the founding ordinance as given by Quinn and Roberds. If challenged, note that the threshold and its enforcement changed over time.
1683 receipts as 'central bank money': this is Quinn and Roberds' interpretation, already flagged as Contested. Defend it as their argument, not as a consensus.
1610 short-selling ban: Petram describes it as a ban on selling shares not owned, which was repeatedly reissued and only partly enforced. Do not call it effective.
Holland interest rates of about 4 percent: this simplifies a gradual decline, with conversions around 1655. Keep 'around' and 'mid-1600s'.
Loans to the VOC: they grew in the 1780s, and the agio went negative around 1790. Avoid giving exact sums.

issues.problem: "In 1609 Amsterdam built the most trusted money in Europe" is an unsourced superlative, and it gets the timing wrong. The bank was founded in 1609, but its reputation and the agio built up over the following decades. It was not the most trusted money in Europe at founding.
issues.fix: "In 1609 Amsterdam founded a bank whose money became some of the most trusted in Europe."

issues.problem: "Two centuries later it lent that trust to a failing company" stretches the timeline. From 1609 to the 1780s is about 175 years.
issues.fix: "Nearly two centuries later it lent that trust to a failing company."
